In [[mathematics]], [[algebra over a field|algebras]] ''A'', ''B'' over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] ''k'' inside some [[field extension]] <math>\Omega</math> of ''k'' are said to be '''linearly disjoint over ''k''''' if the following equivalent conditions are met:
*(i) The map <math>A \otimes_k B \to AB</math> induced by <math>(x, y) \mapsto xy</math> is [[injective]].
*(ii) Any ''k''-[[basis (linear algebra)|basis]] of ''A'' remains [[linearly independent]] over ''B''.
*(iii) There exists a ''k''-[[basis (linear algebra)|basis]] of ''A'' which remains [[linearly independent]] over ''B''.<ref name="Bourbaki_AV14">{{cite book |last1=Bourbaki |first1=N. |author-link=Nicolas Bourbaki |title=Elements of Mathematics, Algebra II, Chapters 4-7 |date=1990 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |page=A.V. 14}}</ref>
*(iv) If <math>u_i, v_j</math> are ''k''-bases for ''A'', ''B'', then the products <math>u_i v_j</math> are linearly independent over ''k''.

Note that, since every subalgebra of <math>\Omega</math> is a [[integral domain|domain]], (i) implies <math>A \otimes_k B</math> is a domain (in particular [[reduced ring|reduced]]). Conversely if ''A'' and ''B'' are fields and either ''A'' or ''B'' is an [[algebraic extension]] of ''k'' and <math>A \otimes_k B</math> is a domain then it is a field and ''A'' and ''B'' are linearly disjoint. However, there are examples where <math>A \otimes_k B</math> is a domain but ''A'' and ''B'' are not linearly disjoint: for example, ''A'' = ''B'' = ''k''(''t''), the [[field of rational functions]] over ''k''.

One also has: ''A'', ''B'' are linearly disjoint over ''k'' [[if and only if]] the subfields of <math>\Omega</math> generated by <math>A, B</math>, resp. are linearly disjoint over ''k''. (cf. [[Tensor product of fields]])

Suppose ''A'', ''B'' are linearly disjoint over ''k''. If <math>A' \subset A</math>, <math>B' \subset B</math> are subalgebras, then <math>A'</math> and <math>B'</math> are linearly disjoint over ''k''. Conversely, if any finitely generated subalgebras of algebras ''A'', ''B'' are linearly disjoint, then ''A'', ''B'' are linearly disjoint (since the condition involves only finite sets of elements.)

Let <math>C</math> be an algebra over a field <math>k</math>, and let <math>U, V</math> be subspaces of <math>C</math>; then <math>U</math> and <math>V</math> are said to be linearly disjoint over <math>K</math> if for any linearly independent elements <math>u_i</math> in <math>U</math> and <math>v_j</math> in <math>V</math>, the elements <math>u_i v_j</math> in <math>C</math> are linearly independent over <math>k</math>. Clearly this just means that the natural mapping <math>U \otimes V \to C</math> induced by the mapping <math>(u, v) \mapsto u v</math> is injective. Now the criterion can be stated as follows: PROPOSITION 5.2 Let <math>C</math> be an algebra over a field <math>k</math>. Given subalgebras <math>A, B</math> of <math>C</math>, if (i) <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are linearly disjoint, (ii) <math>AB = C</math> and (iii) <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> commute elementwise, then <math>C \cong A \otimes B</math>.}}
